title: Assam Minister's ULFA Remarks Spark Row, Sarma Issues Clarification
excerpt: Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said Biswajit Daimary meant the pro-talks ULFA faction that signed the 2023 peace accord, not the banned ULFA-Independent.
body:
• Assam minister Biswajit Daimary faced criticism after remarks in Tinsukia appeared to praise ULFA, the United Liberation Front of Asom.
  • Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma clarified on Thursday that Daimary meant the pro-talks faction led by Anup Chetia, not the banned Paresh Baruah-led ULFA-Independent.
  • The pro-talks faction signed a tripartite peace accord on December 29, 2023, renouncing violence and disbanding; ULFA-I remains banned under UAPA.
  • The Assam Pradesh Mahila Congress wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah seeking an examination of the full speech; Daimary has not issued a separate public statement.

Assam Sports Minister Biswajit Daimary is facing criticism over remarks in which he appeared to praise the United Liberation Front of Asom (ULFA), prompting Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma to step in with a clarification on Thursday, NEInsider reported. The dispute turns on a distinction the chief minister said is central: which ULFA faction the minister was talking about.

What the minister said

Speaking at a public programme in Tinsukia district on Wednesday, Daimary described ULFA as a strong force that had shaped Assam's political course over the past five decades, NEInsider reported. He said the outfit had played a part in stopping outsiders from taking control of the state and, while conceding that some of its actions had drawn criticism, argued that its place in Assam's history should be acknowledged.

He also spoke about the role of the Moran and Muttock communities in the organisation, saying members of these communities had made a large contribution to its leadership, NEInsider reported. IANS, via HiIndia, reported a similar account: Daimary praised ULFA for protecting Assam from outside forces over the past five decades at a gathering in Tinsukia, and highlighted the role of the Moran and Matak communities.

The chief minister's clarification

Responding in Tinsukia on Thursday, Sarma said he had spoken to Daimary about the context of the remarks, NEInsider reported. According to the chief minister, Daimary was referring to the ULFA faction led by Anup Chetia, which came forward for talks and signed a peace agreement with the government, and not to the Paresh Baruah-led ULFA (Independent), which remains banned.

HiIndia's IANS report carried the same clarification. Sarma said the distinction was important because the pro-talks faction had entered a peace agreement and was no longer operating as a banned militant organisation, while ULFA-I remained banned, and that Daimary's comments should not be interpreted as support for ULFA-I.

The 2023 peace accord

Both reports date the agreement to December 2023. NEInsider said the pro-talks faction signed a tripartite peace accord with the Centre and the Assam government in December 2023, after which it was formally disbanded, while ULFA (I) continues to be outlawed under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.

IANS gave the precise date and terms: on December 29, 2023, the Centre, the Assam government and representatives of the pro-talks ULFA faction signed a tripartite Memorandum of Settlement in New Delhi, under which the faction committed to renouncing violence, surrendering arms and ammunition, disbanding its armed organisation and joining the democratic process. ULFA-I, led by Paresh Baruah, remained outside that agreement.

Opposition response

The Assam Pradesh Mahila Congress demanded an explanation from the minister, NEInsider reported. Its leader Meera Borthakur Goswami wrote to Union Home Minister Amit Shah, pointing out that ULFA is banned under UAPA and asking the Centre to examine the full speech. She also asked whether the remarks reflected the state government's official position.

That letter is the reason the clarification matters beyond wording. If a serving minister is heard to praise a banned organisation, the opposition can ask whether policy has changed. Sarma's answer, as reported by both outlets, is that it has not: the faction that signed the accord is distinct from ULFA-I, which remains proscribed.

What to watch

Daimary has not issued a separate public statement on the controversy so far, NEInsider reported. Readers can follow the Assam government through its reported clarification and any response from the Centre to the Congress letter. Whether Daimary speaks directly, and whether the Home Ministry responds, will decide whether the row closes with the chief minister's explanation or continues.
